title: Single Responsibility
summary: A class should have one reason to change. Split the ones that do everything.

steps.title: One reason to change
body: The **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)**: a class should have **one reason to change**, meaning it answers to one kind of requirement.
public int Total() => Sales.Sum();                    // business rule
public string ToCsv() => string.Join(",", Sales);     // formatting

Three different people can ask for a change here: finance changes how totals work, a partner wants JSON instead of CSV, ops moves files to cloud storage. Each change risks breaking the others, and every test of `Total` drags file I/O along.
"Responsibility" is not "does one thing". It is "serves one master".

steps.prompt: Which change request would **not** touch the formatting code in `Report`?
steps.explain: That is a business-rule change. With SRP, it would touch only the class that owns the rule.

steps.title: Splitting it
body: Give each reason to change its own class:
public string Format(SalesLedger ledger) => string.Join(",", ledger.Sales);
public void Save(string path, string text) => File.WriteAllText(path, text);
Each class is small, named for its job, and testable without the others. `SalesLedger` can be tested with no files and no strings.

steps.prompt: Which responsibility does each method belong to?
A class called `UserManager` creates users, hashes passwords, sends emails and writes audit logs. What is the strongest smell?
options: It has several unrelated reasons to change
It has more than three methods
steps.explain: The name is a hint, but the real problem is the many reasons to change. Hashing, email and auditing each deserve their own class.

steps.prompt: Match each class to its single responsibility.
pairs: Turns a password into a hash

steps.prompt: Arrange the high-level `Register` so it delegates each responsibility in turn.
lines: public void Register(string email, string password)
steps.explain: You need the hash before you can build the user, and you store the user before announcing it.

steps.title: Split the report
prompt: `Report` mixes the rule (total) with formatting. Split it, keeping behaviour:
- `class SalesLedger` with `public List<int> Sales { get; } = new();` and `public int Total()`
- `class CsvFormatter` with `public string Format(SalesLedger ledger)` returning e.g. `10,20,30;total=60`
Delete `Report`. The tests use only the two new classes.
starter: public string ToCsv() => string.Join(",", Sales) + ";total=" + Total();
solution: public string Format(SalesLedger ledger) => string.Join(",", ledger.Sales) + ";total=" + ledger.Total();
template: Dojo.Eq("Format of an empty ledger", ";total=0", new CsvFormatter().Format(new SalesLedger()));
